items.q: (A) No sooner the bell had rung than the students, (B) most of whom had barely slept, (C) poured into the corridor, (D) eager to compare answers.
options: No sooner the bell had rung than the students,
most of whom had barely slept,
items.correction: No sooner had the bell rung than the students,
items.explanation: After the negative adverbial No sooner at the start of a sentence, the auxiliary and subject invert: No sooner had the bell rung than.

items.q: The coach (A) insisted that every player (B) attends the dawn training session, (C) regardless of how far (D) they lived from the stadium.
items.correction: attend the dawn training session,
items.explanation: After verbs of demand such as insist, demand, suggest, the that-clause takes the subjunctive base form: insisted that every player attend.

items.q: (A) Having missed the last ferry by minutes, (B) the hikers had little choice (C) but sleeping on the pier (D) until dawn.
options: Having missed the last ferry by minutes,
items.correction: but to sleep on the pier
items.explanation: The fixed pattern is have (little/no) choice but + to-infinitive: had little choice but to sleep.

items.q: (A) Had the council listened to the engineers (B) a decade ago, (C) the old bridge (D) will not be crumbling now.
options: Had the council listened to the engineers
items.correction: would not be crumbling now.
items.explanation: A mixed conditional pairs an unreal past condition (Had the council listened) with an unreal present result, which needs would + verb, not will.

items.q: (A) A great deal of researches (B) into sleep patterns (C) has been carried out (D) on teenagers rather than on adults.
options: on teenagers rather than on adults.
items.correction: A great deal of research
items.explanation: Research is uncountable, so it has no plural and combines with a great deal of; the singular verb has been carried out confirms this.

items.q: The lecture was (A) delivered in (B) so a monotonous voice (C) that half the audience (D) had dozed off before the first slide changed.
options: had dozed off before the first slide changed.
items.correction: such a monotonous voice
items.explanation: Before a + adjective + noun use such (such a monotonous voice); so only works in the inverted form so monotonous a voice.

items.q: (A) Scarcely had the orchestra (B) played the opening bars (C) than a mobile phone rang (D) somewhere in the back rows.
items.correction: when a mobile phone rang
items.explanation: Scarcely/Hardly ... when is the correct pairing; than belongs only with No sooner.

items.q: The northern valleys receive (A) plentiful rain throughout the year, (B) whereas the southern plains (C) remain parched (D) despite of lying only fifty kilometres away.
options: despite of lying only fifty kilometres away.
items.correction: despite lying only fifty kilometres away.
items.explanation: Despite is already a preposition and never takes of; say despite lying or in spite of lying.

items.q: (A) It was not until the final whistle blew when (B) the goalkeeper realised (C) she had been playing (D) with a fractured finger.
options: It was not until the final whistle blew when
items.correction: It was not until the final whistle blew that
items.explanation: A cleft sentence with It was not until ... is completed by that, never when: It was not until the whistle blew that she realised.

items.q: (A) If only the museum (B) would have kept its original opening hours, (C) we could have seen the exhibition (D) before it closed for good.
options: would have kept its original opening hours,
we could have seen the exhibition
items.correction: had kept its original opening hours,
items.explanation: A regret about the past after if only / wish takes the past perfect (had kept); would have is not used in the if-only clause.

items.q: The new principal is admired (A) for her patience, (B) for her wit, and (C) because she is fair (D) in every dispute she settles.
items.correction: for her fairness
items.explanation: Items in a list must be parallel: two for + noun phrases cannot be followed by a because clause, so use for her fairness.

items.q: (A) Unwilling to admit defeat, (B) the chess prodigy (C) studied the position for an hour (D) before finally resign.
options: studied the position for an hour
items.correction: before finally resigning.
items.explanation: After the preposition before a verb must take the -ing form: before finally resigning.

items.q: (A) Under no circumstances the reactor should be restarted (B) until the inspectors, (C) who arrive tomorrow, (D) have signed off on the repairs.
options: Under no circumstances the reactor should be restarted
have signed off on the repairs.
items.correction: Under no circumstances should the reactor be restarted
items.explanation: A fronted negative phrase such as Under no circumstances forces subject-auxiliary inversion: should the reactor be restarted.

items.q: The residents (A) demanded that the airline (B) is held accountable (C) for the noise (D) its night flights generate over the suburbs.
options: its night flights generate over the suburbs.
items.correction: be held accountable
items.explanation: Demand that introduces a subjunctive clause, so the passive uses the bare be: demanded that the airline be held accountable.

items.q: Despite months of negotiation, (A) the two ministers admitted (B) it was (C) strongly unlikely (D) that a treaty would be signed before the election.
options: that a treaty would be signed before the election.
items.correction: highly unlikely
items.explanation: The natural intensifier for unlikely is highly (or extremely); strongly collocates with verbs like recommend or disagree, not with unlikely.

items.q: (A) If the river were not (B) so heavily polluted, (C) the festival organisers (D) would hold the swimming race there last summer.
options: would hold the swimming race there last summer.
items.correction: would have held the swimming race there last summer.
items.explanation: This mixed conditional has a present condition and a past result (last summer), so the result clause needs would have held.

items.q: (A) Walking along the cliff path at dusk, (B) the lighthouse came into view (C) far sooner (D) than we had expected.
options: Walking along the cliff path at dusk,
items.correction: we saw the lighthouse come into view
items.explanation: A dangling participle: the subject of the main clause must be the one doing the walking, so it has to be we, not the lighthouse.

items.q: (A) Fewer equipment than expected (B) survived the flood, (C) which left the laboratory (D) unable to resume its experiments for weeks.
options: unable to resume its experiments for weeks.
items.correction: Less equipment than expected
items.explanation: Equipment is uncountable, so it takes less; fewer is reserved for plural countable nouns.

items.q: (A) Not until the last guest had left (B) did the host admit (C) that she has been feeling unwell (D) all evening.
options: Not until the last guest had left
that she has been feeling unwell
items.correction: that she had been feeling unwell
items.explanation: The admission is reported in the past (did the host admit), so a state that continued up to that point takes the past perfect continuous: had been feeling.

items.q: (A) Although the kick-off was pushed back (B) by nearly two hours, (C) the visiting fans (D) sang while the whole delay without a single complaint.
options: Although the kick-off was pushed back
sang while the whole delay without a single complaint.
items.correction: sang throughout the whole delay without a single complaint.
items.explanation: While is a conjunction and must introduce a clause; before a noun phrase such as the whole delay use the preposition throughout or during.

items.q: (A) Despite she was one of the youngest entrants, (B) Linh delivered her speech (C) with a composure (D) that many adults would envy.
options: Despite she was one of the youngest entrants,
items.correction: Although she was one of the youngest entrants,
items.explanation: Despite is a preposition and cannot govern a full clause; a subject + verb needs the conjunction although (or despite being).

items.q: (A) Neither the referee (B) nor the linesmen was aware (C) that the ball had crossed the line (D) a full second earlier.
options: that the ball had crossed the line
items.correction: nor the linesmen were aware
items.explanation: With neither ... nor the verb agrees with the nearer subject; the linesmen is plural, so the verb is were.

items.q: The storm, (A) which meteorologists had tracked for a week, (B) made landfall near a town (C) where its harbour had only just been rebuilt (D) after the previous winter's floods.
options: which meteorologists had tracked for a week,
where its harbour had only just been rebuilt
items.correction: whose harbour had only just been rebuilt
items.explanation: Possession inside a relative clause is expressed with whose; where its doubles up the reference and leaves the clause without a proper link.

items.q: (A) The astronaut told reporters (B) that she had felt (C) strangely calm during re-entry and (D) that she will gladly fly again the following year.
options: that she will gladly fly again the following year.
items.correction: that she would gladly fly again the following year.
items.explanation: In reported speech after a past reporting verb, will backshifts to would; the following year confirms the shifted time frame.

items.q: (A) The most carefully you read the contract, (B) the fewer surprises you are likely (C) to encounter (D) once the work begins.
options: The most carefully you read the contract,
the fewer surprises you are likely
items.correction: The more carefully you read the contract,
items.explanation: A double comparative uses two comparatives, not a superlative: The more carefully ..., the fewer ....

items.q: (A) The committee praised (B) whomever had designed the poster, (C) though nobody (D) came forward to claim the credit.
options: came forward to claim the credit.
items.correction: whoever had designed the poster,
items.explanation: The pronoun is the subject of had designed inside its own clause, so it must be whoever; the case is decided by the clause, not by the verb praised.

items.q: (A) Few would deny (B) that access to (C) the clean water is (D) a right rather than a privilege.
options: a right rather than a privilege.
items.correction: clean water is
items.explanation: An uncountable noun used in a general sense takes no article: access to clean water, not the clean water.

items.q: (A) The rapid expansion of the city (B) has placed enormous strain (C) on its ageing and (D) increasingly unreliable infrastructural.
options: The rapid expansion of the city
items.correction: increasingly unreliable infrastructure.
items.explanation: After the adjectives ageing and unreliable a noun is required; infrastructural is itself an adjective, and the noun is infrastructure.

items.q: (A) Renowned by its glassblowers, (B) the island town (C) attracts craftsmen (D) who travel from as far afield as Japan.
options: who travel from as far afield as Japan.
items.correction: Renowned for its glassblowers,
items.explanation: The adjective renowned (like famous and known) takes for when naming what something is admired for.

items.q: (A) Only after the lab results came back (B) the doctors realised (C) how close the patient (D) had come to losing her sight.
options: Only after the lab results came back
had come to losing her sight.
items.correction: did the doctors realise
items.explanation: When a sentence opens with Only after + clause, the main clause inverts: did the doctors realise.

items.q: (A) The volunteers will begin (B) clearing the beach (C) as soon as the tide will have gone out (D) far enough to expose the rocks.
options: as soon as the tide will have gone out
far enough to expose the rocks.
items.correction: as soon as the tide has gone out
items.explanation: In a time clause introduced by as soon as, future meaning is expressed with the present (perfect), never with will: as soon as the tide has gone out.

items.q: (A) The migrating cranes (B) made such little noise (C) crossing the marsh (D) that the birdwatchers heard only the wind.
options: that the birdwatchers heard only the wind.
items.correction: made so little noise
items.explanation: When little is the quantifier meaning not much, it is intensified with so (so little noise ... that); such little would mean small in size.

items.q: (A) The documentary, (B) shot over three winters, (C) follows a herd of reindeer (D) as they migrating across the tundra.
options: as they migrating across the tundra.
items.correction: as they migrate across the tundra.
items.explanation: A clause after the conjunction as needs a finite verb; the bare participle migrating has no auxiliary, so use migrate (or are migrating).

items.q: (A) I wish I listened (B) to my grandmother's advice (C) about saving (D) when I still had a steady income.
options: when I still had a steady income.
items.correction: I wish I had listened
items.explanation: Wish about a past event (when I still had a steady income) takes the past perfect: I wish I had listened.

items.q: (A) What impressed the judges most (B) was not the robot's speed (C) but how quick it recovered (D) after being knocked over.
items.correction: but how quickly it recovered
items.explanation: The word modifies the verb recovered, so it must be the adverb quickly; the adjective quick can only describe a noun.

items.q: (A) The bakery on the corner (B) has built up a loyal following (C) over two decades (D) by keeping an open eye on quality.
options: has built up a loyal following
by keeping an open eye on quality.
items.correction: by keeping a close eye on quality.
items.explanation: The idiom for careful monitoring is keep a close eye on (or keep an eye on); an open eye is not an English collocation.

items.q: (A) Hardly the plane had taken off (B) when the turbulence began, (C) sending trays (D) sliding down the aisle.
options: Hardly the plane had taken off
items.correction: Hardly had the plane taken off
items.explanation: Sentence-initial Hardly triggers inversion of the auxiliary and subject: Hardly had the plane taken off when ....

items.q: (A) The number of students (B) who cycle to school have doubled (C) since the council (D) opened the riverside lane.
options: who cycle to school have doubled
items.correction: who cycle to school has doubled
items.explanation: The number of + plural noun is a singular subject, so the main verb is has doubled; only a number of takes a plural verb.

items.q: (A) Although the guide (B) gave us (C) a few useful advice (D) about tipping, we still felt awkward in restaurants.
options: about tipping, we still felt awkward in restaurants.
items.correction: some useful advice
items.explanation: Advice is uncountable, so a few is impossible; use some, a little or a piece of useful advice.

items.q: (A) Faced with a mounting deficit, (B) the theatre (C) had no choice but to (D) cut back in its free matinees for schoolchildren.
options: cut back in its free matinees for schoolchildren.
items.correction: cut back on its free matinees for schoolchildren.
items.explanation: The phrasal verb meaning to reduce is cut back on something; in is not part of the idiom.
